rounds.text: Franklin Leasing & Finance Ltd is trading at a steep discount to its asset backing, with a price-to-book ratio of just 0.37x based on a share price of ₹ 8.91 and a book value of ₹ 24.1 [E2]. This valuation is exceptionally cheap when compared against the sector benchmark price-to-book ratio of 1.35x [E7]. The underlying business possesses a proven ability to scale over longer horizons, delivering a consistent compounded sales growth rate of 18% over both 10-year and 5-year periods [E14, E15], which even outpaces the sector median sales growth of 16.6% [E64]. Furthermore, the company is showing fundamental operational improvement as recent profit growth exceeds one-year price growth by 14%, indicating that the business is starting to outperform expectations [E50]. Conceded: [E1], [E4], [E6], [E16], [E17].

Franklin Leasing & Finance Ltd trades at an exorbitant price-to-earnings ratio of 82.7, which towers massively over the sector benchmark of 20.02x [E1, E6]. This premium valuation is entirely disconnected from its operational reality, evidenced by a completely nonexistent dividend yield of 0.00% [E4]. Furthermore, the company's top-line growth has severely deteriorated in the near term, demonstrating a compounded sales contraction of 7% over 3 years and a steeper 29% decline over the trailing twelve months [E16, E17]. Conceded: the company boasts a low price-to-book ratio of 0.37x alongside a 10-year and 5-year compounded sales growth rate of 18% [E2, E14, E15]. However, these historical metrics offer cold comfort when weighed against an anemic return on assets of 0% compared to a sector benchmark of 1.83% [E8]. Ultimately, investors are paying a fourfold sector multiple for a shrinking business that fails to generate meaningful asset returns or distribute cash [E1, E6, E8, E17].

The bull highlights a low price-to-book ratio of 0.37x against a sector benchmark of 1.35x [E2, E7], but this asset backing is undermined by a complete failure to generate operational returns, with an ROA of 0% compared to the sector benchmark of 1.83% [E8]. While the bull cites historical 5-year and 10-year compounded sales growth of 18% [E14, E15], this long-term view obscures a severe recent contraction, evidenced by a 3-year compounded sales growth of -7% and a trailing twelve-month collapse of -29% [E16, E17]. Conceded: [E64]. The bull points to recent profit growth exceeding 1-year price growth by 14% [E50], yet this metric sits alongside a punitive trailing P/E of 82.7x and a sector-dwarfing 81x multiple [E1, E6] that makes the stock extraordinarily expensive on an earnings basis. Finally, the total absence of a dividend yield at 0.00% [E4] and a stagnant stock sitting just 28% up its 52-week range [E5] show that investors are receiving no cash return while holding a business experiencing severe near-term revenue decay.
